clue.text: Supplies hose to cover end of street

indicators.note: the socks cover the T, wrapping round it
takes the final letter of 'street'

explanation.surface: A shop restocks its hosiery while a street market winds down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hose' looks like a garden hose; here it is legwear, the socks that wrap round the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Stocks are supplies kept on hand, as in a shop's stocks of goods.

clue.text: Cast actors in charge of teaching method

definitions.note: SOCRATIC is an adjective, used as in 'the Socratic method'; the clue's phrase names the method itself.

indicators.note: to cast is to throw about, so the letters of ACTORS are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A drama teacher decides who plays which part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast actors' reads as theatre casting; 'Cast' is the instruction to rearrange ACTORS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Socratic method teaches by asking a pupil a chain of questions, as Socrates did.

clue.text: Fatefully, oxygen present in O- likely discharged

indicators.note: the O for oxygen sits inside the word MINUS
likely is emptied of its contents, leaving only its outer letters

blocks.note: the blood group O- is read out as 'O minus'
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen, placed inside MINUS to make MINOUS

explanation.surface: A hospital worries over a patient with a rare blood group who may be sent home.
explanation.walkthrough: The symbol 'O-' has to be spoken as 'O minus'; the oxygen then goes inside MINUS, giving O MIN(O)US before LY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ominously means in a way that bodes ill, as if fate were signalling what is coming.

clue.text: Philosophical German soldier supporting King

indicators.note: in a down entry, the ANT goes beneath the K and holds it up

explanation.surface: A German infantryman stands loyal to his monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German soldier' looks like one unit; 'German' belongs to the definition and the soldier is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: Immanuel Kant, author of the Critique of Pure Reason, was the great philosopher of 18th-century Königsberg in Prussia.

clue.text: Vintage Popeye in film recording that needs to be refined

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause describing the answer: crude oil is the stuff that needs refining.

indicators.note: a recording is something heard, so the phrase is taken by sound

blocks.note: a cru is a wine of a classed vintage; Popeye Doyle is the detective in the film The French Connection

explanation.surface: An old Popeye cartoon reel is due for restoration.
explanation.walkthrough: Popeye is not the sailor but Gene Hackman's detective 'Popeye' Doyle in The French Connection; 'cru Doyle' said quickly gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude oil is petroleum as it comes out of the ground, which must be refined before use.

clue.text: Fierce diatribe about current measure

indicators.note: the rant goes around the AMP

blocks.note: the amp is the unit of electric current

explanation.surface: Someone rails furiously about electricity readings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' suggests the present day; here it is electric current, measured in amps.
explanation.definitionFit: Rampant can mean fierce and unrestrained, like a rampant lion rearing to attack.

clue.text: Husband opening food store in megacity

indicators.note: the H forms an opening in the shop, splitting it

blocks.note: a deli is a food shop

explanation.surface: A married man opens a grocery in a huge city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' reads as a man opening his shop for business; it means the H splits DELI open, DEL-H-I.
explanation.definitionFit: Delhi, with its tens of millions of inhabitants, is one of the world's megacities.

clue.text: Fine beer served up for African resident

indicators.note: in a down entry, 'up' turns IPA to read upwards as API

blocks.note: IPA = India pale ale, a beer

explanation.surface: A bar in Africa serves a local a decent pint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'African resident' sounds like a person; it is an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The okapi, a striped relative of the giraffe, lives in the forests of central Africa.

clue.text: Vigorous appetite, yen

explanation.surface: A list of words for a hearty desire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' could mean longing, a synonym for appetite; here it is the Japanese currency, abbreviated Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Lusty means healthy and vigorous, as in a lusty cry.

clue.text: Reportedly ready for American anguish

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: 'ready' is British slang for cash; the American's cash is the dollar

explanation.surface: Someone is said to be prepared to take on an American's pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is not prepared but British slang for money (as in 'the readies'), so the American's ready is the dollar.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolour is a literary word for grief or anguish.

clue.text: Organic bananas repelling Mr Munro?

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters of ORGANIC go wild
to repel is to drive back, so MR is sent backwards

explanation.surface: Organic fruit keeps a man called Munro at bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr Munro' looks like a man's name; 'Mr' is wordplay and a Munro is a Scottish mountain over 3,000 feet. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Cairn Gorm, in the Scottish Highlands, is one of the Munros.

clue.text: Starts to look enquiringly at Keir Starmer's dodgy briefings

indicators.note: take the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Journalists begin to probe unofficial briefings from the UK Prime Minister's team.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer is the British Labour Prime Minister; only his initials matter here.
explanation.definitionFit: A leak is information passed unofficially to the press, a dodgy kind of briefing.

clue.text: Answer negative from Macron immediately

blocks.note: 'non' is French for no; Emmanuel Macron is the French president

explanation.surface: The French president gives a flat no without hesitation.
explanation.walkthrough: Macron stands for France, so his negative is NON. Anon now usually means 'soon', but its older sense is 'at once'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon originally meant straightaway, immediately, as in Shakespeare.

clue.text: Turbulence until embraced by very old non-clerics

indicators.note: to be embraced is to be held in someone's arms, so TIL is held within LAITY

blocks.note: the laity are people who are not clergy
til is a short form of until, placed inside LAITY: LA-TIL-ITY

explanation.surface: Upheaval lasts until the elderly congregation takes things in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-clerics' is a roundabout way to say the laity, ordinary church members as opposed to clergy; 'til' is the informal short form of until.
explanation.definitionFit: Volatility is instability or turbulence, as in markets or moods.

clue.text: Boy unsheathed sword

indicators.note: the sword has its outer covering removed, losing its first and last letters

blocks.note: BLADE loses its outer letters B and E

explanation.surface: A boy draws a sword from its scabbard.
explanation.walkthrough: The sword is a BLADE, and stripping its outside leaves LAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lad is an informal word for a boy or young man.

clue.text: Papers eviscerated leftie disliking work

indicators.note: to eviscerate is to remove the insides, leaving only the outer letters

explanation.surface: Newspapers savage a work-shy left-winger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' suggests the press; it is identity papers, ID.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone idle is lazy and averse to work.

clue.text: Privileged individual jailed, back in Dartmoor

indicators.note: the back of Dartmoor is its last letter

explanation.surface: A well-connected person ends up behind bars back at Dartmoor.
explanation.walkthrough: Dartmoor is a well-known English prison, which makes 'back in Dartmoor' read as a return to jail.
explanation.definitionFit: An insider is someone with privileged access to an organisation.

clue.text: Retired in Toulouse, D'Artagnan deals in financial products

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the hidden letters read backwards
the answer lies inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: D'Artagnan, the musketeer, retires to Toulouse and plays the markets.
explanation.walkthrough: The run SEDART spans the break between the two names; read backwards it gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To trade is to buy and sell, here in financial products such as stocks.

clue.text: Swear nothing concealed by Head of Audi (German car firm)

indicators.note: the O is hidden inside VW
take the first letter of Audi

explanation.surface: An executive at Audi swears nothing is being hidden by the parent carmaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket reads as an explanation of Audi; it is its own piece of wordplay, VW, which Audi's owner happens to be.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to avow is to state openly and solemnly, as one does under oath.

clue.text: Remember wee Kenny securing a fast time?

indicators.note: the outer words hold the answer fast inside them

explanation.surface: Someone recalls young Kenny winning a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast time' sounds like a race time; it is a period of fasting, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Ember weeks are the weeks containing the Ember days, set aside in the Church calendar for fasting and prayer.

clue.text: Strong and solid ending for Babes in the Wood

indicators.note: take the last letter of Babes
the S goes inside the wood

blocks.note: a thicket is a dense wood
last letter of BabeS, placed inside THICKET

explanation.surface: A sturdy ending is promised for the pantomime Babes in the Wood.
explanation.walkthrough: Babes in the Wood is a traditional British Christmas pantomime; the title is split so that its last letter of 'Babes' goes in a THICKET.
explanation.definitionFit: Thickset describes a heavy, solidly built, strong-looking body.

clue.text: My clue shocked college

indicators.note: a shock jolts the letters of MY CLUE into a new order

explanation.surface: The setter's own clue has scandalised a college.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter talking about 'my clue' is a playful nudge that the clue's own words are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyceum is a school or college, after Aristotle's Lyceum in Athens.

clue.text: Vehicle air-conditioning turned on, heading for Rye

indicators.note: AC is turned round to CA, and 'on' puts it on top of the next piece
take the first letter of Rye

explanation.surface: A driver switches on the air-con on the way to the town of Rye.
explanation.walkthrough: Rye is a small town in Sussex, England; 'turned on' reads as switching on but reverses AC.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the car is the commonest road vehicle.

clue.text: In Germany with little sister, occupied by ordinary division of cells

indicators.note: the O takes up a place inside MITSIS

explanation.surface: Someone in Germany travels with a younger sibling, busy with everyday life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Germany' asks for the German word for 'with'; 'ordinary' as O is a crossword abbreviation from exam grades (O level).
explanation.definitionFit: Mitosis is the kind of cell division that produces two identical daughter cells.

clue.text: Bear periodically brash pompous official

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter of brash

blocks.note: B, A, H: letters 1, 3 and 5 of BrAsH

explanation.surface: Someone must put up with a loud, self-important official from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' reads as a verb, to put up with; it is the noun, Pooh.
explanation.definitionFit: Pooh-Bah, from Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, stands for a self-important official holding many posts.

clue.text: Pair from Australia caught importing advanced drug

indicators.note: PROZC brings the A inside it

blocks.note: A = advanced, as in A level

explanation.surface: Two Australians are arrested smuggling a narcotic.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a drug bust, and the drug really is the answer. Oz is the informal name for Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Prozac is the brand name of the antidepressant drug fluoxetine.

clue.text: My pro unit arranged bribery

indicators.note: the letters of PRO UNIT are put into a new order

blocks.note: 'Cor!' and 'My!' are both exclamations of surprise

explanation.surface: A professional squad has set up a bribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is not a possessive but an exclamation, like the British 'cor!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: bribery is one kind of corruption, the dishonest use of power for gain.

clue.text: Boorish character, vacuous idiot

indicators.note: empty, so character keeps only its outer letters

explanation.surface: A description of a loutish figure: an empty-headed fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacuous idiot' reads as one phrase; 'vacuous' actually empties 'character', leaving CR.
explanation.definitionFit: Crass means coarse and insensitive, boorish.

clue.text: A few drinks and a sandwich

blocks.note: the set of drinks one person buys for the whole group at the pub
in Britain, a sandwich made from two whole slices of bread is counted as one of these

explanation.surface: An order at the pub: some drinks and something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a 'round of sandwiches' is one sandwich; buying a round is buying drinks for everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a set of drinks for the group and a single sandwich are called a round.

clue.text: Turn over page, captivated by Dune novel

indicators.note: the P is held captive inside the rearranged DUNE
novel means new, so DUNE takes a new form

blocks.note: DUNE rearranged, with the P placed inside

explanation.surface: A reader flips a page, gripped by Frank Herbert's science-fiction novel Dune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like it names Dune as a book; it is the instruction to rearrange its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To upend something is to turn it over or upside down.

clue.text: Reptile beginning to chase enormous bird

indicators.note: take the first letter of chase

blocks.note: the roc is a giant bird of Arabian legend

explanation.surface: A crocodile starts to stalk a huge bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The roc is the monstrous bird of the Sinbad stories, a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: Crocodiles are reptiles, and croc is the everyday clipped form of the word.

clue.text: Newspaper article featuring European cheese

indicators.note: FT A includes the E as a feature

explanation.surface: A newspaper runs a feature on a European cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newspaper article' reads as one thing, a piece in the paper; it is two pieces, FT and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: feta is a crumbly brined Greek cheese made from sheep's or goat's milk.

clue.text: Maltreat stand-in brought round in A&E

indicators.note: SUB is turned round to BUS
'in' places one thing within another, so BUS sits within A and E

blocks.note: A&E is a British hospital's accident and emergency department
a sub is a substitute, turned round to BUS and placed in A&E

explanation.surface: A locum doctor is mistreated after being revived in the emergency department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought round' reads as revived from unconsciousness, which suits an emergency ward; it means turned back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to maltreat someone is to treat them badly, which is the verb abuse.

clue.text: Connery's identical, to a smaller extent brazen

indicators.note: Sean Connery's famous slushy S turns 'same' into 'shame' when he says it

explanation.surface: A comment on Sean Connery: much the same, just a bit less bold.
explanation.walkthrough: Sean Connery, the first film James Bond, is famous for pronouncing S as SH.
explanation.definitionFit: Shameless means brazen, without any sense of shame.

clue.text: Small fish tail from pilchard is hot accompaniment

indicators.note: take the last letter of pilchard

blocks.note: the ide is a freshwater fish
H = hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A menu note: a small fish tail from a pilchard is a spicy garnish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small fish' looks like one item; S and IDE are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A side dish is served to accompany a main course.

clue.text: Mum runs drug shop in America

blocks.note: ket is slang for the drug ketamine

explanation.surface: A mother operates a pharmacy in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' reads as a verb for managing the shop; it is R. 'Drug shop' suggests a pharmacy, but the definition is 'shop in America'.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage a market is a food shop or grocery store.
